entries.28dc0099cb3870cbf75b0b085bf2e6a2cdd454f7: <div sID="gen1579" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Exod.8" sID="Exod.8"/> <div eID="gen1579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1580" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen1581" type="x-p"/> Three more of the plagues of Egypt are related in this chapter, I. That of the frogs, which is, 1. Threatened, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. 2. Inflicted, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.5-Exod.8.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. 3. Mimicked by the magicians, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.7">ver. 7</reference>. 4. Removed, at the humble request of Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.8-Exod.8.14">ver. 8-14</reference>), who yet hardens his heart, and, notwithstanding his promise while the plague was upon him (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.8">ver. 8</reference>), refuses to let Israel go, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.15">ver. 15</reference>. II. The plague of lice (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.16-Exod.8.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>), by which, 1. The magicians were baffled (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.18-Exod.8.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>), and yet, 2. Pharaoh was hardened, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.19">ver. 19</reference>. III. That of flies. 1. Pharaoh is warned of it before (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.20-Exod.8.21">ver. 20, 21</reference>), and told that the land of Goshen should be exempt from this plague, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.22-Exod.8.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. 2. The plague is brought, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.24">ver. 24</reference>. 3. Pharaoh treats with Moses about the release of Israel, and humbles himself, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.25-Exod.8.29">ver. 25-29</reference>. 4. The plague is thereupon removed (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.31">ver. 31</reference>), and Pharaoh's heart hardened, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.32">ver. 32</reference>.
entries.f1f869a74884f55cdf2f3654a62515be337990b8: <div eID="gen1581" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen1580" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Plagues of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen1582" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, Go unto Pharaoh, and say unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Let my people go, that they may serve me. <hi type="super">2</hi> And if thou refuse to let <hi type="italic">them</hi> go, behold, I will smite all thy borders with frogs: <hi type="super">3</hi> And the river shall bring forth frogs abundantly, which shall go up and come into thine house, and into thy bedchamber, and upon thy bed, and into the house of thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thine ovens, and into thy kneadingtroughs: <hi type="super">4</hi> And the frogs shall come up both on thee, and upon thy people, and upon all thy servants. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch forth thine hand with thy rod over the streams, over the rivers, and over the ponds, and cause frogs to come up upon the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the magicians did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, Intreat the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he may take away the frogs from me, and from my people; and I will let the people go, that they may do sacrifice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And Moses said unto Pharaoh, Glory over me: when shall I intreat for thee, and for thy servants, and for thy people, to destroy the frogs from thee and thy houses, <hi type="italic">that</hi> they may remain in the river only? <hi type="super">10</hi> And he said, To morrow. And he said, <hi type="italic">Be it</hi> according to thy word: that thou mayest know that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the frogs shall depart from thee, and from thy houses, and from thy servants, and from thy people; they shall remain in the river only. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh: and Moses cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> because of the frogs which he had brought against Pharaoh. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did according to the word of Moses; and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the villages, and out of the fields. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they gathered them together upon heaps: and the land stank. <hi type="super">15</hi> But when Pharaoh saw that there was respite, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had said. <div eID="gen1582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1583" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh is here first threatened and then plagued with frogs, as afterwards, in this chapter, with lice and flies, little despicable inconsiderable animals, and yet by their vast numbers rendered sore plagues to the Egyptians. God could have plagued them with lions, or bears, or wolves, or with vultures or other birds of prey; but he chose to do it by these contemptible instruments. 1. That he might magnify his own power. He is Lord of the hosts of the whole creation, has them all at his beck, and makes what use he pleases of them. Some have thought that the power of God is shown as much in the making of an ant as in the making of an elephant; so is his providence in serving his own purposes by the least creatures as effectually as by the strongest, that the excellency of the power, in judgment as well as mercy, may be of God, and not of the creature. See what reason we have to stand in awe of this God, who, when he pleases, can arm the smallest parts of the creation against us. If God be our enemy, all the creatures are at war with us. 2. That he might humble Pharaoh's pride, and chastise his insolence. What a mortification must it needs be to this haughty monarch to see himself brought to his knees, and forced to submit, by such despicable means! Every child is, ordinarily, able to deal with those invaders, and can triumph over them; yet now so numerous were their troops, and so vigorous their assaults, that Pharaoh, with all his chariots and horsemen, could make no head against them. Thus he <hi type="italic">poureth contempt upon princes</hi> that offer contempt to him and his sovereignty, and makes those who will not own him above them to know that, when he pleases, he can make the meanest creature to insult them and trample upon them. As to the plague of frogs we may observe, <div eID="gen1583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1584" type="x-p"/> I. How it was threatened. Moses, no doubt, attended the divine Majesty daily for fresh instructions, and (perhaps while the river was yet blood) he is here directed to give notice to Pharaoh of another judgment coming upon him, in case he continue obstinate: <hi type="italic">If thou refuse to let them go,</hi> it is at thy peril, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Note, God does not punish men for sin unless they persist in it. <hi type="italic">If he turn not, he will whet his sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.12">Ps. vii. 12</reference>), which implies favour <hi type="italic">if he turn.</hi> So here, <hi type="italic">If thou refuse, I will smite thy borders,</hi> intimating that if Pharaoh complied the controversy should immediately be dropped. The plague threatened, in case of refusal, was formidably extensive. Frogs were to make such an inroad upon them as should make them uneasy in their houses, in their beds, and at their tables; they should not be able to eat, nor drink, nor sleep in quietness, but, wherever they were, should be infested by them, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.3-Exod.8.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Note, 1. God's curse upon a man will pursue him wherever he goes, and lie heavily upon him whatever he does. See <reference osisRef="Deut.28.16">Deut. xxviii. 16</reference>, &c. 2. There is no avoiding divine judgments when they invade with commission. <div eID="gen1584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1585" type="x-p"/> II. How it was inflicted. Pharaoh not regarding the alarm, nor being at all inclined to yield to the summons, Aaron is ordered to draw out the forces, and with his outstretched arm and rod to give the signal of battle. <hi type="italic">Dictum factum—No sooner said then done;</hi> the host is mustered, and, under the direction and command of an invisible power, shoals of frogs invade the land, and the Egyptians, with all their art and all their might, cannot check their progress, nor so much as give them a diversion. Compare this with that prophecy of an army of locusts and caterpillars, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joel ii. 2</reference>, &c.; and see <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16-Isa.34.17">Isa. xxxiv. 16, 17</reference>. Frogs came up, at the divine call, and <hi type="italic">covered the land.</hi> Note, God has many ways of disquieting those that live at ease. <div eID="gen1585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1586" type="x-p"/> III. How the magicians were permitted to imitate it, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.7">v. 7</reference>. They also brought up frogs, but could not remove those that God sent. The unclean spirits which came <hi type="italic">out of the mouth of the dragon</hi> are said to be like frogs, which go forth to the kings of the earth, to deceive them (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.13">Rev. xvi. 13</reference>), which probably alludes to these frogs, for it follows the account of the turning of the waters into blood. The dragon, like the magicians, intended by them to deceive, but God intended by them to destroy those that would be deceived. <div eID="gen1586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1587" type="x-p"/> IV. How Pharaoh relented under this plague: it was the first time he did so, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.8">v. 8</reference>. He begs of Moses to intercede for the removal of the frogs, and promises fair that he will let the people go. He that a little while ago had spoken with the utmost disdain both of God and Moses is now glad to be beholden to the mercy of God and the prayers of Moses. Note, Those that bid defiance to God and prayer in a day of extremity will, first or last, be made to see their need of both, and will cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">Matt. vii. 22</reference>. Those that have bantered prayer have been brought to beg it, as the rich man that had scorned Lazarus courted him for a drop of water. <div eID="gen1587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1588" type="x-p"/> V. How Moses fixes the time with Pharaoh, and then prevails with God by prayer for the removal of the frogs. Moses, to show that his performances had no dependence upon the conjunctions or oppositions of the planets, or the luckiness of any one hour more than another, bids Pharaoh name his time. <hi type="italic">Nellum occurrit tempus regi—No time fixed on by the king shall be objected to,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.8.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Have thou this honour over me,</hi> tell me <hi type="italic">against when I shall entreat for thee.</hi> This was designed for Pharaoh's conviction, that, if his eyes were not opened by the plague, they might by the removal of it. So various are the methods God takes to bring men to repentance. Pharaoh sets the time for <hi type="italic">to-morrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.8.10">v. 10</reference>. And why not immediately? Was he so fond of his guests that he would have them stay another night with him? No, but probably he hoped that they would go away of themselves, and then he should get clear of the plague without being obliged either to God or Moses. However, Moses joins issue with him upon it: "<hi type="italic">Be it according to thy word,</hi> it shall be done just when thou wouldst have it done, <hi type="italic">that thou mayest know that,</hi> whatever the magicians pretend to, <hi type="italic">there is none like unto the Lord our God.</hi> None has such a command as he has over all the creatures, nor is any one so ready to forgive those that humble themselves before him." Note, The great design both of judgments and mercies is to convince us that there is none like the Lord our God, none so wise, so mighty, so good, no enemy so formidable, no friend so desirable, so valuable. Moses, hereupon, applies to God, prays earnestly to him, to remand the frogs, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.12">v. 12</reference>. Note, We must pray for our enemies and persecutors, even the worst as Christ did. In answer to the prayer of Moses, the frogs that came up one day perished the next, or the next but one. They all died (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.13">v. 13</reference>), and, that it might appear that they were real frogs, their dead bodies were left to be raked together in heaps, so that the smell of them became offensive, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.14">v. 14</reference>. Note, The great Sovereign of the world makes what use he pleases of the lives and deaths of his creatures; and he that gives a being, to serve one purpose, may, without wrong to his justice, call for it again immediately, to serve another purpose. <div eID="gen1588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1589" type="x-p"/> VI. What was the issue of this plague (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">When Pharaoh saw there was a respite,</hi> without considering either what he had lately felt or what he had reason to fear, he hardened his heart. Note, 1. Till the heart is renewed by the grace of God, the impressions made by the force of affliction do not abide; the convictions wear off, and the promises that were extorted are forgotten. Till the disposition of the air is changed, what thaws in the sun will freeze again in the shade. 2. God's patience is shamefully abused by impenitent sinners. The respite he gives them, to lead them to repentance, they are hardened by; and while he graciously allows them a truce, in order to the making of their peace, they take that opportunity to rally again the baffled forces of an obstinate infidelity. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Eccl. viii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.34">Ps. lxxviii. 34</reference>, &c.
entries.51acd515b2061b84da1555d90dc3596bd819989a: <div eID="gen1589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1590" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Say unto Aaron, Stretch out thy rod, and smite the dust of the land, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they did so; for Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod, and smote the dust of the earth, and it became lice in man, and in beast; all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the magicians did so with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not: so there were lice upon man, and upon beast. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then the magicians said unto Pharaoh, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the finger of God: and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them; as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had said. <div eID="gen1590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1591" type="x-p"/> Here is a short account of the plague of lice. It does not appear that any warning was given of it before. Pharaoh's abuse of the respite granted to him might have been a sufficient warning to him to expect another plague: for if the removal of an affliction harden us, and so we lose the benefit of it, we may conclude it goes away with a purpose to return or to make room for a worse. Observe, <div eID="gen1591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1592" type="x-p"/> I. How this plague of lice was inflicted on the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.16-Exod.8.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. The frogs were produced out of the waters, but these live out of <hi type="italic">the dust of the earth;</hi> for out of any part of the creation God can fetch a scourge, with which to correct those that rebel against him. He has many arrows in his quiver. Even the dust of the earth obeys him. "<hi type="italic">Fear not then, thou worm Jacob,</hi> for God can use thee as a threshing instrument, if he please," <reference osisRef="Isa.41.14-Isa.41.15">Isa. xli. 14, 15</reference>. These lice, no doubt, were extremely vexatious, as well as scandalous, to the Egyptians. Though they had respite, they had respite but awhile, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.14">Rev. xi. 14</reference>. The second woe was past, but behold the third woe came very quickly. <div eID="gen1592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1593" type="x-p"/> II. How the magicians were baffled by it, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.18">v. 18</reference>. They attempted to imitate it, but they could not. When they failed in this, it should seem they attempted to remove it; for it follows, <hi type="italic">So there were lice upon man and beast,</hi> in spite of them. This forced them to confess themselves overpowered: <hi type="italic">This is the finger of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.19">v. 19</reference>); that is, "This check and restraint put upon us must needs be from a divine power." Note, 1. God has the devil in a chain, and limits him both as a deceiver and as a destroyer; <hi type="italic">hitherto he shall come, but no further.</hi> The devil's agents when God permitted them, could do great things; but when he laid an embargo upon them, though but with his finger, they could do nothing. The magicians' inability, in this less instance, showed whence they had their ability in the former instances which seemed greater, and that they had no power against Moses but what was given them from above. 2. Sooner or later God will extort, even from his enemies, an acknowledgment of his own sovereignty and over-ruling power. It is certain they must all (as we say) knock under at last, as Julian the apostate did, when his dying lips confessed, <hi type="italic">Thou hast overcome me, O thou Galilean!</hi> God will not only be too hard for all opposers, but will force them to own it. <div eID="gen1593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1594" type="x-p"/> III. How Pharaoh, notwithstanding this, was made more and more obstinate (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.19">v. 19</reference>); even those that had deceived him now said enough to undeceive him, and yet he grew more and more obstinate. Even the miracles and the judgments were to him a savour of death unto death. Note, Those that are not made better by God's word and providences are commonly made worse by them.
entries.745753cac405ae2dc616ddf460a0aa435fa5b801: <div eID="gen1594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Rise up early in the morning, and stand before Pharaoh; lo, he cometh forth to the water; and say unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Let my people go, that they may serve me. <hi type="super">21</hi> Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms <hi type="italic">of flies</hi> upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms <hi type="italic">of flies,</hi> and also the ground whereon they <hi type="italic">are.</hi> <hi type="super">22</hi> And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms <hi type="italic">of flies</hi> shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the midst of the earth. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will put a division between my people and thy people: to morrow shall this sign be. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did so; and there came a grievous swarm <hi type="italic">of flies</hi> into the house of Pharaoh, and <hi type="italic">into</hi> his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt: the land was corrupted by reason of the swarm <hi type="italic">of flies.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And Pharaoh called for Moses and for Aaron, and said, Go ye, sacrifice to your God in the land. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Moses said, It is not meet so to do; for we shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God: lo, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, and will they not stone us? <hi type="super">27</hi> We will go three days' journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, as he shall command us. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Pharaoh said, I will let you go, that ye may sacrifice to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God in the wilderness; only ye shall not go very far away: intreat for me. <hi type="super">29</hi> And Moses said, Behold, I go out from thee, and I will intreat the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that the swarms <hi type="italic">of flies</hi> may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, to morrow: but let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more in not letting the people go to sacrifice to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses went out from Pharaoh, and intreated the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did according to the word of Moses; and he removed the swarms <hi type="italic">of flies</hi> from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; there remained not one. <hi type="super">32</hi> And Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also, neither would he let the people go. <div eID="gen1595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1596" type="x-p"/> Here is the story of the plague of flies, in which we are told, <div eID="gen1596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1597" type="x-p"/> I. How it was threatened, like that of frogs, before it was inflicted. Moses is directed (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.20">v. 20</reference>) to rise early in the morning, to meet Pharaoh when he came forth to the water, and there to repeat his demands. Note, 1. Those that would bring great things to pass for God and their generation must rise early, and redeem time in the morning. Pharaoh was early up at his superstitious devotions to the river; and shall we be for more sleep and more slumber when any service is to be done which would pass well in our account in the great day? 2. Those that would approve themselves God's faithful servants must not be afraid of the face of man. Moses must <hi type="italic">stand before Pharaoh,</hi> proud as he was, and tell him that which was in the highest degree humbling, must challenge him (if he refused to release his captives) to engage with any army of flies, which would obey God's orders of Pharaoh would not. See a similar threatening, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa. vii. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord will hiss</hi> (or whistle) <hi type="italic">for the fly and the bee,</hi> to come and serve his purposes. <div eID="gen1597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1598" type="x-p"/> II. How the Egyptians and the Hebrews were to be remarkably distinguished in this plague, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.22-Exod.8.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. It is probable that this distinction had not been so manifest and observable in any of the foregoing plagues as it was to be in this. Thus, as the plague of lice was made more convincing than any before it, by its running the magicians aground, so was this, by the distinction made between the Egyptians and the Hebrews. Pharaoh must be made to know that <hi type="italic">God is the Lord in the midst of the earth;</hi> and by this it will be known beyond dispute. 1. Swarms of flies, which seem to us to fly at random, shall be manifestly under the conduct of an intelligent mind, while they are above the direction of any man. "Hither they shall go," says Moses, "and thither they shall not come;" and the performance is punctually according to this appointment, and both, compared, amount to a demonstration that he that said it and he that did it was the same, even a Being of infinite power and wisdom. 2. The servants and worshippers of the great Jehovah shall be preserved from sharing in the common calamities of the place they live in, so that the plague which annoys all their neighbours shall not approach them; and this shall be an incontestable proof that God is <hi type="italic">the Lord in the midst of the earth.</hi> Put both these together, and it appears that <hi type="italic">the eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the earth,</hi> and through the air too, to direct that which to us seems most casual, to serve some great designed end, that he may <hi type="italic">show himself strong on the behalf of those whose hearts are upright with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2 Chron. xvi. 9</reference>. Observe how it is repeated: <hi type="italic">I will put a division between my people and thy people</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.8.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, The Lord knows those that are his, and will make it appear, perhaps in this world, certainly in the other, that he has set them apart for himself. A day will come when you shall <hi type="italic">return and discern between the righteous and the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">the sheep and the goats</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">Matt. xxv. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Ezek. xxxiv. 17</reference>), though now intermixed. <div eID="gen1598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1599" type="x-p"/> III. How it was inflicted, the day after it was threatened: <hi type="italic">There came a grievous swarm of flies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.24">v. 24</reference>), flies of divers sorts, and such as devoured them, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.45">Ps. lxxviii. 45</reference>. The prince of the power of the air has gloried in being <hi type="italic">Beelzebub—the god of flies;</hi> but here it is proved that even in <hi type="italic">that</hi> he is a pretender and a usurper, for even with swarms of flies God fights against his kingdom and prevails. <div eID="gen1599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1600" type="x-p"/> IV. How Pharaoh, upon this attack, sounded a parley, and entered into a treaty with Moses and Aaron about a surrender of his captives: but observe with what reluctance he yields. <div eID="gen1600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1601" type="x-p"/> 1. He is content they should sacrifice to their God, provided they would do it in the land of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, God can extort a toleration of his worship, even from those that are really enemies to it. Pharaoh, under the smart of the rod, is content they should do sacrifice, and will allow liberty of conscience to God's Israel, even in his own land. But Moses will not accept his concession; he cannot do it, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.26">v. 26</reference>. It would be an abomination to God should they offer the Egyptian sacrifices, and an abomination to the Egyptians should they offer to God their own sacrifices, as they ought; so that they could not sacrifice in the land without incurring the displeasure either of their God or of their task-masters; therefore he insists: <hi type="italic">We will go three days' journey into the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.8.27">v. 27</reference>. Note, Those that would offer an acceptable sacrifice to God must, (1.) Separate themselves from the wicked and profane; for we cannot have fellowship both with the Father of lights and with the works of darkness, both with Christ and with Belial, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.14 Ps.26.4">2 Cor. vi. 14, &c.</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 4, 6</reference>. (2.) They must retire from the distractions of the world, and get as far as may be from the noise of it. Israel cannot keep the feast of the Lord either among the brick-kilns or among the flesh-pots of Egypt; no, <hi type="italic">We will go into the wilderness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.14">Hos. ii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.7.11">Cant. vii. 11</reference>. (3.) They must observe the divine appointment: "We will sacrifice as God shall command us, and not otherwise." Though they were in the utmost degree of slavery to Pharaoh, yet in the worship of God, they must observe his commands and not Pharaoh's. <div eID="gen1601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1602" type="x-p"/> 2. When this proposal is rejected, he consents for them to go into the wilderness, provided they do not go <hi type="italic">very far away,</hi> not so far but that he might fetch them back again, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.28">v. 28</reference>. It is probable he had heard of their design upon Canaan, and suspected that if once they left Egypt they would never come back again; and therefore, when he is forced to consent that they shall go (the swarms of flies buzzing the necessity in his ears), yet he is not willing that they should go out of his reach. Thus some sinners who, in a pang of conviction, part with their sins, yet are loth they should go very far away; for, when the fright is over, they will return to them again. We observe here a struggle between Pharaoh's convictions and his corruptions; his convictions said, "Let them go;" his corruptions said, "Yet not very far away:" but he sided with his corruptions against his convictions, and this was his ruin. This proposal Moses so far accepted as that he promised the removal of this plague upon it, <reference osisRef="Exod.8.29">v. 29</reference>. See here, (1.) How ready God is to accept sinners' submissions. Pharaoh does but say, <hi type="italic">Entreat for me</hi> (though it is with regret that he humbles so far), and Moses promises immediately, <hi type="italic">I will entreat the Lord for thee,</hi> that Pharaoh might see what the design of the plague was, not to bring him to ruin, but to bring him to repentance. With what pleasure did God say (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.29">1 Kings xxi. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">Seest thou how Ahab humbles himself?</hi> (2.) What need we have to be admonished that we be sincere in our submission: <hi type="italic">But let not Pharaoh deal deceitfully any more.</hi> Those that deal deceitfully are justly suspected, and must be cautioned not to return again to folly, after God has once more spoken peace. <hi type="italic">Be not deceived, God is not mocked;</hi> if we think to put a cheat upon God by a counterfeit repentance, and a fraudulent surrender of ourselves to him, we shall prove, in the end, to have put a fatal cheat upon our own souls. <div eID="gen1602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1603" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The issue of all was that God graciously removed the plague (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.30-Exod.8.31">v. 30, 31</reference>), but Pharaoh perfidiously returned to his hardness, and <hi type="italic">would not let the people go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.8.32">v. 32</reference>. His pride would not let him part with such a flower of his crown as his dominion over Israel was, nor his covetousness with such a branch of his revenue as their labours were. Note, Reigning lusts break through the strongest bounds, and make men impudently presumptuous and scandalously perfidious. Let not sin therefore reign; for, if it do, it will betray and hurry us to the grossest absurdities.  <chapter eID="Exod.8"/> <div eID="gen1603" type="x-p"/>

entries.27735061ae8757e718740febf27f00cea1c112c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv652"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.15">Ex 8:1-15</reference>. Plague of Frogs.</title> <div sID="gen929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv652"/><hi type="bold">1. the Lord spake unto Moses, Go unto Pharaoh--</hi>The duration of the first plague for a whole week must have satisfied all that it was produced not by any accidental causes, but by the agency of omnipotent power. As a judgment of God, however, it produced no good effect, and Moses was commanded to wait on the king and threaten him, in the event of his continued obstinacy, with the infliction of a new and different plague. As Pharaoh's answer is not given, it may be inferred to have been unfavorable, for the rod was again raised. <div eID="gen929" type="x-p"/>
entries.471a281f0593e73b775925db1ddea21cd4dca501: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv653"/><div sID="gen930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv653"/><hi type="bold">2. I will smite all thy borders with frogs--</hi>Those animals, though the natural spawn of the river, and therefore objects familiar to the people, were on this occasion miraculously multiplied to an amazing extent, and it is probable that the ova of the frogs, which had been previously deposited in the mire and marshes, were miraculously brought to perfection at once. <div eID="gen930" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d0a67aeccb5e7df50b42ae6a5b1858447122d03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv654"/><div sID="gen931" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv654"/><hi type="bold">3. bedchamber ... bed--</hi>mats strewed on the floor as well as more sumptuous divans of the rich.<div eID="gen931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen932" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ovens--</hi>holes made in the ground and the sides of which are plastered with mortar.<div eID="gen932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kneading-troughs--</hi>Those used in Egypt were bowls of wicker or rush work. What must have been the state of the people when they could find no means of escape from the cold, damp touch and unsightly presence of the frogs, as they alighted on every article and vessel of food! <div eID="gen933" type="x-p"/>
entries.81f1c33feb1b667dd6fc95dab5fe773680de1ab2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv655"/><div sID="gen934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv655"/>5-6. Stretch forth thine hand with thy rod over the streams, &c. The miracle consisted in the reptiles leaving their marshes at the very time he commanded them. <div eID="gen934" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcb6b75d550e993ce9458457c79dcb0bc2002cb5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv656"/><div sID="gen935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv656"/><hi type="bold">7. the magicians did so with their enchantments--</hi>required no great art to make the offensive reptiles appear on any small spot of ground. What they undertook to do already existed in abundance all around. They would better have shown their power by removing the frogs. <div eID="gen935" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f50870ad9b69c8431a48b062e536c9dac1b886b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv657"/><div sID="gen936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv657"/><hi type="bold">8-15. Pharaoh called, ... Intreat the Lord, that he may take away the frogs from me--</hi>The frog, which was now used as an instrument of affliction, whether from reverence or abhorrence, was an object of national superstition with the Egyptians, the god Ptha being represented with a frog's head. But the vast numbers, together with their stench, made them an intolerable nuisance so that the king was so far humbled as to promise that, if Moses would intercede for their removal, he would consent to the departure of Israel, and in compliance with this appeal, they were withdrawn at the very hour named by the monarch himself. But many, while suffering the consequences of their sins, make promises of amendment and obedience which they afterwards forget; and so Pharaoh, when he saw there was a respite, was again hardened [Ex 8:15]. <div eID="gen936" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7ea22555689111e8804a2b05b5ae4536c4e89a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv658"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.8.16-Exod.8.19">Ex 8:16-19</reference>. Plague of Lice.</title> <div sID="gen937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv658"/><hi type="bold">16. smite the dust of the land, &c.--</hi>Aaron's rod, by the direction of Moses, who was commanded by God, was again raised, and the land was filled with gnats, mosquitoes--that is the proper meaning of the original term. In ordinary circumstances they embitter life in Eastern countries, and therefore the terrible nature of this infliction on Egypt may be imagined when no precautions could preserve from their painful sting. The very smallness and insignificance of these fierce insects made them a dreadful scourge. The magicians never attempted any imitation, and what neither the blood of the river nor the nuisance of the frogs had done, the visitation of this tiny enemy constrained them to acknowledge "this is the finger of God"--properly "gods," for they spoke as heathens. <div eID="gen937" type="x-p"/>
entries.4de653096aebc069f274bc710aa36b67ef72c91f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv659"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.8.20-Exod.8.32">Ex 8:20-32</reference>. Plague of Flies.</title> <div sID="gen938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv659"/><hi type="bold">20-24. Rise up early ... Pharaoh; lo, he cometh forth to the water, &c.--</hi>Pharaoh still appearing obdurate, Moses was ordered to meet him while walking on the banks of the Nile and repeat his request for the liberation of Israel, threatening in case of continued refusal to cover every house from the palace to the cottage with swarms of flies--while, as a proof of the power that accomplished this judgment, the land of Goshen should be exempted from the calamity. The appeal was equally vain as before, and the predicted evil overtook the country in the form of what was not "flies," such as we are accustomed to, but divers sorts of flies (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.45">Psa 78:45</reference>), the gad fly, the cockroach, the Egyptian beetle, for all these are mentioned by different writers. They are very destructive, some of them inflicting severe bites on animals, others destroying clothes, books, plants, every thing. The worship of flies, particularly of the beetle, was a prominent part of the religion of the ancient Egyptians. The employment of these winged deities to chastise them must have been painful and humiliating to the Egyptians while it must at the same time have strengthened the faith of the Israelites in the God of their fathers as the only object of worship. <div eID="gen938" type="x-p"/>
entries.78b80bba4eae1033590e9cd0d4a33639f6d0adea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv660"/><div sID="gen939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv660"/><hi type="bold">25-32. Pharaoh called for Moses, ... Go ye, sacrifice to your God in the land, &c.--</hi>Between impatient anxiety to be freed from this scourge and a reluctance on the part of the Hebrew bondsmen, the king followed the course of expediency; he proposed to let them free to engage in their religious rites within any part of the kingdom. But true to his instructions, Moses would accede to no such arrangement; he stated a most valid reason to show the danger of it, and the king having yielded so far as to allow them a brief holiday across the border, annexed to this concession a request that Moses would entreat with Jehovah for the removal of the plague. He promised to do so, and it was removed the following day. But no sooner was the pressure over than the spirit of Pharaoh, like a bent bow, sprang back to its wonted obduracy, and, regardless of his promise, he refused to let the people depart. <chapter eID="Exod.8"/>

entries.c6e9cf7850bfb1b5c05adb47fa522d2a3053b003: <div eID="gen2597" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen2598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2600" type="x-p"/> The plague of frogs threatened, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.1">Exo 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.2">Exo 8:2</reference>. The extent of this plague, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.3">Exo 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.4">Exo 8:4</reference>. Aaron commanded to stretch out his hand, with the rod, over the river and waters of Egypt, in consequence of which the frogs came, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.5">Exo 8:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.6">Exo 8:6</reference>. The magicians imitate this miracle, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.7">Exo 8:7</reference>. Pharaoh entreats Moses to remove the frogs, and promises to let the people go, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.8">Exo 8:8</reference>. Moses promises that they shall be removed from every part of Egypt, the river excepted, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.9-Exo.8.11">Exo 8:9-11</reference>. Moses prays to God, and the frogs die throughout the land of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.12-Exo.8.14">Exo 8:12-14</reference>. Pharaoh, finding himself respited, hardens his heart, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.15">Exo 8:15</reference>. The plague of lice on man and beast, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.16">Exo 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.17">Exo 8:17</reference>. The magicians attempt to imitate this miracle, but in vain, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.18">Exo 8:18</reference>. They confess it to be the finger of God, and yet Pharaoh continues obstinate, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.19">Exo 8:19</reference>. Moses is sent again to him to command him to let the people go, and in case of disobedience he is threatened with swarms of flies, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.20">Exo 8:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.21">Exo 8:21</reference>. A promise made that the land of Goshen, where the Israelites dwelt, should be exempted front this plague, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.22">Exo 8:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.23">Exo 8:23</reference>. The flies are sent, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.24">Exo 8:24</reference>. Pharaoh sends for Moses and Aaron, and offers to permit them to sacrifice in the land, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.25">Exo 8:25</reference>. They refuse, and desire to go three days' journey into the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.26">Exo 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.27">Exo 8:27</reference>. Pharaoh consents to let them go a little way, provided they would entreat the Lord to remove the flies, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.28">Exo 8:28</reference>. Moses consents, prays to God, and the flies are removed, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.29-Exo.8.31">Exo 8:29-31</reference>. After which Pharaoh yet hardened his heart, and refused to let the people go, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.32">Exo 8:32</reference>. <div eID="gen2600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2601" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen2601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2602" type="x-p"/> Let my people go - God, in great mercy to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, gives them notice of the evils he intended to bring upon them if they continued in their obstinacy. Having had therefore such warning, the evil might have been prevented by a timely humiliation and return to God.
entries.ae9d071d89c25ec02b74ae6762169cb9402d2535: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen2602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2603" type="x-p"/> If thou refuse - Nothing can be plainer than that Pharaoh had it still in his power to have dismissed the people, and that his refusal was the mere effect of his own wilful obstinacy. <div eID="gen2603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2604" type="x-p"/> With frogs - צפרדעים tsepardeim. This word is of doubtful etymology: almost all interpreters, both ancient and modern, agree to render it as we do, though some mentioned by Aben Ezra think the crocodile is meant; but these can never weigh against the conjoint testimony of the ancient versions. Parkhurst derives the word from צפר tsaphar, denoting the brisk action, or motion of the light, and ידע yada, to feel, as they seem to feel or rejoice in the light, croaking all the summer months, yet hiding themselves in the winter. The Arabic name for this animal is very nearly the same with the Hebrew zafda, where the letters are the same, the ר resch being omitted. It is used as a quadriliteral root in the Arabic language, to signify froggy, or containing frogs: see Golius. But the true etymology seems to be given by Bochart, who says the word is compounded of zifa, a bank, and rada, mud, because the frog delights in muddy or marshy places; and that from these two words the noun zafda is formed, the re being dropped. In the Batrocho myomachia of Homer, the frog has many of its epithets from this very circumstance. Hence Λιμνοχαρις, delighting in the lake; Βορβοροκοιτης, lying or engendering in the mud; Πηλευς, and Πηλβατης, belonging to the mud, walking in the mud, etc., etc. <div eID="gen2604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2605" type="x-p"/> A frog is in itself a very harmless animal; but to most people who use it not as an article of food, exceedingly loathsome. God, with equal ease, could have brought crocodiles, bears, lions, or tigers to have punished these people and their impious king, instead of frogs, lice, flies, etc. But had he used any of those formidable animals, the effect would have appeared so commensurate to the cause, that the hand of God might have been forgotten in the punishment; and the people would have been exasperated without being humbled. In the present instance he shows the greatness of his power by making an animal, devoid of every evil quality, the means of a terrible affliction to his enemies. How easy is it, both to the justice and mercy of God, to destroy or save by means of the most despicable and insignificant of instruments! Though he is the Lord of hosts he has no need of powerful armies, the ministry of angels, or the thunderbolts of justice, to punish a sinner or a sinful nation; the frog or the fly in his hands is a sufficient instrument of vengeance.
entries.f57c4e25ed482c1839b4483f4b7ed7ad0281f2da: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen2605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2606" type="x-p"/> The river shall bring forth frogs abundantly - The river Nile, which was an object of their adoration, was here one of the instruments of their punishment. The expression, bring forth abundantly, not only shows the vast numbers of those animals, which should now infest the land, but it seems also to imply that all the spawn or ova of those animals which were already in the river and marshes, should be brought miraculously to a state of perfection. We may suppose that the animals were already in an embryo existence, but multitudes of them would not have come to a state of perfection had it not been for this miraculous interference. This supposition will appear the more natural when it is considered that the Nile was remarkable for breeding frogs, and such other animals as are principally engendered in such marshy places as must be left in the vicinity of the Nile after its annual inundations. <div eID="gen2606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2607" type="x-p"/> Into thine ovens - In various parts of the east, instead of what we call ovens they dig a hole in the ground, in which they insert a kind of earthen pot, which having sufficiently heated, they stick their cakes to the inside, and when baked remove them and supply their places with others, and so on. To find such places full of frogs when they came to heat them, in order to make their bread, must be both disgusting and distressing in the extreme.
entries.5984308ee2ea4dc5eceb90de7e9c801d53211967: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen2607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2608" type="x-p"/> Stretch forth thine hand - over the streams, over the rivers - The streams and rivers here may refer to the grand divisions of the Nile in the Lower Egypt, which were at least seven, and to the canals by which these were connected; as there were no other streams, etc., but what proceeded from this great river.
entries.99230e678abb5fc850a0748ba0d21d395be47418: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen2608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2609" type="x-p"/> The frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt - In some ancient writers we have examples of a similar plague. The Abderites, according to Orosius, and the inhabitants of Paeonia and Dardania, according to Athenaeus, were obliged to abandon their country on account of the great numbers of frogs by which their land was infested.
entries.e92f00078a0836cb9c134700257e540dc0a7366b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen2609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2610" type="x-p"/> The magicians did so - A little juggling or dexterity of hand might have been quite sufficient for the imitation of this miracle, because frogs in abundance had already been produced; and some of these kept in readiness might have been brought forward by the magicians, as proofs of their pretended power and equality in influence to Moses and Aaron.
entries.ec6a4106cfac63ec100798aed3801e1d7b1a7aa1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen2610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2611" type="x-p"/> Glory over me - התפאר עלי hithpaer alai. These words have greatly puzzled commentators in general; and it is not easy to assign their true meaning. The Septuagint render the words thus: Ταξαι προς με ποτε, etc., Appoint unto me when I shall pray, etc. The constitue mihi quando of the Vulgate is exactly the same; and in this sense almost all the versions understood this place. This countenances the conjectural emendation of Le Clerc, who, by the change of a single letter, reading התבאר hithbaer for התפאר hithpaer, gives the same sense as that in the ancient versions. Houbigant, supposing a corruption in the original, amends the reading thus: אתה באר עלי attah baar alai - Dic mihi quo tempore, etc., "Tell me when thou wishest me to pray for thee," etc., which amounts to the same in sense with that proposed by Le Clerc. Several of our English versions preserve the same meaning; so in the Saxon Heptateuch; so in Becke's Bible, 1549, "And Moses sayed unto Pharaoh, Appoint thou the time unto me." This appears to be the genuine import of the words, and the sense taken in this way is strong and good. We may conceive Moses addressing Pharaoh in this way: "That thou mayest be persuaded that Jehovah alone is the inflicter of these plagues, appoint the time when thou wouldst have the present calamity removed, and I will pray unto God, and thou shalt plainly see from his answer that this is no casual affliction, and that in continuing to harden thy heart and resist thou art sinning against God." Nothing could be a fuller proof that this plague was supernatural than the circumstance of Pharaoh's being permitted to assign himself the time of its being removed, and its removal at the intercession of Moses according to that appointment. And this is the very use made of it by Moses himself, <reference osisRef="Exo.8.10">Exo 8:10</reference>, when he says, Be it according to thy word: that thou mayest know that there is none like unto the Lord our God; and that, consequently, he might no longer trust in his magicians, or in his false gods.
entries.6d3bff94ae576ab283a73f415bd6da6eb1d30420: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen2611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2612" type="x-p"/> They gathered them together upon heaps - The killing of the frogs was a mitigation of the punishment; but the leaving them to rot in the land was a continual proof that such a plague had taken place, and that the displeasure of the Lord still continued. The conjecture of Calmet is at least rational: he supposes that the plague of flies originated from the plague of frogs; that the former deposited their ova in the putrid masses, and that from these the innumerable swarms afterwards mentioned were hatched. In vindication of this supposition it may be observed, that God never works a miracle when the end can be accomplished by merely natural means; and in the operations of Divine providence we always find that the greatest number of effects possible are accomplished by the fewest causes. As therefore the natural means for this fourth plague had been miraculously provided by the second, the Divine Being had a right to use the instruments which he had already prepared.
entries.6d5fc1aa4eae7f9a925f7bd6112efb5e4cc2f376: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen2612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2613" type="x-p"/> Smite the dust of the land, that it may become lice - If the vermin commonly designated by this name be intended, it must have been a very dreadful and afflicting plague to the Egyptians, and especially to their priests, who were obliged to shave the hair off every part of their bodies, and to wear a single tunic, that no vermin of this kind might be permitted to harbor about them. See Herod. in Euterp., c. xxxvii., p. 104, edit. Gale. Of the nature of these insects it is not necessary to say much. The common louse is very prolific. In the space of twelve days a full-grown female lays one hundred eggs, from which, in the space of six days, about fifty males and as many females are produced. In eighteen days these young females are at their full growth, each of which may lay one hundred eggs, which will be all hatched in six days more. Thus, in the course of six weeks, the parent female may see 5,000 of its own descendants! So mightily does this scourge of indolence and filthiness increase! <div eID="gen2613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2614" type="x-p"/> But learned men are not agreed on the signification of the original word כנים kinnim, which different copies of the Septuagint render σκνιφες, σκνιπες, and σκνηπες, gnats; and the Vulgate renders sciniphes, which signifies the same. <div eID="gen2614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2615" type="x-p"/> Mr. Harmer supposes he has found out the true meaning in the word tarrentes, mentioned by Vinisauf, one of our ancient English writers; who, speaking of the expedition of King Richard I. to the Holy Land, says, that "while the army were marching from Cayphas to Caesarea, they were greatly distressed every night by certain worms called tarrentes, which crept on the ground, and occasioned a very burning heat by most painful punctures; for, being armed with stings, they conveyed a poison which quickly occasioned those who were wounded by them to swell, and was attended with the most acute pain." All this is far fetched. Bochart has endeavored to prove that the כנים kinnim of the text may mean lice in the common acceptation of the term, and not gnats. 1. Because those in question sprang from the dust of the earth, and not from the waters. 2. Because they were both on men and cattle, which cannot be spoken of gnats. 3. Because their name comes from the radix כון kun, which signifies to make firm, fix, establish, which can never agree to gnats, flies, etc., which are ever changing their place, and are almost constantly on the wing. 4. Because כנה kinnah is the term by which the Talmudists express the louse, etc. See his Hierozoicon, vol. ii., c. xviii., col. 571. The circumstance of their being in man and in beast agrees so well with the nature of the acarus sanguisugus, commonly called the tick, belonging to the seventh order of insects called Aptera, that I am ready to conclude this is the insect meant. This animal buries both its sucker and head equally in man or beast; and can with very great difficulty be extracted before it is grown to its proper size, and filled with the blood and juices of the animal on which it preys. When fully grown, it has a glossy black oval body: not only horses, cows, and sheep are infested with it in certain countries, but even the common people, especially those who labor in the field, in woods, etc. I know no insect to which the Hebrew term so properly applies. This is the fixed, established insect, which will permit itself to be pulled in pieces rather than let go its hold; and this is literally באדם ובבהמה baadam ubabbehemah, in man and in beast, burying its trunk and head in the flesh of both. In woodland countries I have seen many persons as well as cattle grievously infested with these insects.
entries.b68fa80c97ec4e028b64c50adaa4eea98b1af80e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen2615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2616" type="x-p"/> The magicians did so - That is, They tried the utmost of their skill, either to produce these insects or to remove this plague; but they could not, no juggling could avail here, because insects must be produced which would stick to and infix themselves in man and beast, which no kind of trick could possibly imitate; and to remove them, as some would translate the passage, was to their power equally impossible. If the magicians even acted by spiritual agents, we find from this case that these agents had assigned limits, beyond which they could not go; for every agent in the universe is acting under the direction or control of the Almighty.
entries.2a4dcaf81b39a039adbe47148e1e99d32072b424: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen2616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2617" type="x-p"/> This is the finger of God - That is, The power and skill of God are here evident. Probably before this the magicians supposed Moses and Aaron to be conjurers, like themselves; but now they are convinced that no man could do these miracles which these holy men did, unless God were with him. God permits evil spirits to manifest themselves in a certain way, that men may see that there is a spiritual world, and be on their guard against seduction. He at the same time shows that all these agents are under his control, that men may have confidence in his goodness and power.
entries.2aee29f01f1e2148dcc0342404aa83127c8f5bd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen2617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2618" type="x-p"/> Swarms of flies upon thee - It is not easy to ascertain the precise meaning of the original word הערב hearob; as the word comes from ערב arab, he mingled, it may be supposed to express a multitude of various sorts of insects. And if the conjecture be admitted that the putrid frogs became the occasion of this plague, (different insects laying their eggs in the bodies of those dead animals, which would soon be hatched, see on <reference osisRef="Exo.8.14">Exo 8:14</reference> (note)), then the supposition that a multitude of different hinds of insects is meant, will seem the more probable. Though the plague of the locusts was miraculous, yet God both brought it and removed it by natural means; see <reference osisRef="Exo.10.13-Exo.10.19">Exo 10:13-19</reference>. <div eID="gen2618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2619" type="x-p"/> Bochart, who has treated this subject with his usual learning and ability, follows the Septuagint, explaining the original by κυνομυια, the dog-fly; which must be particularly hateful to the Egyptians, because they held dogs in the highest veneration, and worshipped Anubis under the form of a dog. In a case of this kind the authority of the Septuagint is very high, as they translated the Pentateuch in the very place where these plagues happened. But as the Egyptians are well known to have paid religious veneration to all kinds of animals and monsters, whence the poet: - <div eID="gen2619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2620" type="x-p"/> Omnigenumque deum monstra, et latrator Anubis, <div eID="gen2620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2621" type="x-p"/> I am inclined to favor the literal construction of the word: for as ערב ereb, <reference osisRef="Exo.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>, expresses that mixed multitude of different kinds of people who accompanied the Israelites in their departure from Egypt; so here the same term being used, it may have been designed to express a multitude of different kinds of insects, such as flies, wasps, hornets, etc., etc. The ancient Jewish interpreters suppose that all kinds of beasts and reptiles are intended, such as wolves, lions, bears, serpents, etc. Mr. Bate thinks the raven is meant, because the original is so understood in other places; and thus he translates it in his literal version of the Pentateuch: but the meaning already given is the most likely. As to the objection against this opinion drawn from <reference osisRef="Exo.8.31">Exo 8:31</reference>, there remained not one, it can have very little weight, when it is considered that this may as well be spoken of one of any of the different kinds, as of an individual of one species.
entries.9c17e74df73682cc3dbafcabd67f6a6c5b71823e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen2621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2622" type="x-p"/> I will sever in that day - הפליתי hiphleythi, has been translated by some good critics, I will miraculously separate; so the Vulgate: Faciam mirabilem, "I will do a marvellous thing." And the Septuagint, παραδοξασω, I will render illustrious the land of Goshen in that day; and this he did, by exempting that land, and its inhabitants the Israelites, from the plagues by which he afflicted the land of Egypt.
entries.b7925856d8d435e4c14266a23312a89a57598504: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen2622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2623" type="x-p"/> And I will put a division - פדת peduth, a redemption, between my people and thy people; God hereby showing that he had redeemed them from those plagues to which he had abandoned the others.
entries.31f66920ce2071fda99ca55e3bae114e0881b126: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen2623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2624" type="x-p"/> The land was corrupted - Every thing was spoiled, and many of the inhabitants destroyed, being probably stung to death by these venomous insects. This seems to be intimated by the psalmist, "He sent divers sorts of flies among them, which Devoured them," <reference osisRef="Psa.78.45">Psa 78:45</reference>. <div eID="gen2624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2625" type="x-p"/> In ancient times, when political, domestic, and personal cleanliness was but little attended to, and offal of different kinds permitted to corrupt in the streets and breed vermin, flies multiplied exceedingly, so that we read in ancient authors of whole districts being laid waste by them; hence different people had deities, whose office it was to defend them against flies. Among these we may reckon Baalzebub, the fly-god of Ekron; Hercules, muscarum abactor, Hercules, the expeller of flies, of the Romans; the Muagrus of the Eleans, whom they invoked against pestilential swarms of flies; and hence Jupiter, the supreme god of the heathens, had the epithets of Απομυιος and Μυωδης, because he was supposed to expel flies, and defend his worshippers against them. See Dodd.
entries.3861888ad40fe9ea38b4f851fad8541fdfc97a8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen2625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2626" type="x-p"/> Sacrifice to your God in the land - That is, Ye shall not leave Egypt, but I shall cause your worship to be tolerated here.
entries.4f7172a000cd01df363124a10bb578437e0dfb04: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen2626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2627" type="x-p"/> We shall sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians - That is, The animals which they hold sacred, and will not permit to be slain, are those which our customs require us to sacrifice to our God; and should we do this in Egypt the people would rise in a mass, and stone us to death. Perhaps few people were more superstitious than the Egyptians. Almost every production of nature was an object of their religious worship: the sun, moon, planets, stars, the river Nile, animals of all sorts, from the human being to the monkey, dog, cat, and ibis, and even the onions and leeks which grew in their gardens. Jupiter was adored by them under the form of a ram, Apollo under the form of a crow, Bacchus under that of a goat, and Juno under that of a heifer. The reason why the Egyptians worshipped those animals is given by Eusebius, viz., that when the giants made war on the gods, they were obliged to take refuge in Egypt, and assume the shapes or disguise themselves under different kinds of animals in order to escape. Jupiter hid himself in the body of a ram, Apollo in that of a crow, Bacchus in a goat, Diana in a cat, Juno in a white heifer, Venus in a fish, and Mercury in the bird ibis; all which are summoned up by Ovid in the following lines: - <div eID="gen2627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2628" type="x-p"/> Duxque gregis fit Jupiter - <div eID="gen2628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2629" type="x-p"/> Delius in corvo, proles Semeleia capro, <div eID="gen2629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2630" type="x-p"/> Fele soror Phoebi, nivea Saturnia vacca, <div eID="gen2630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2631" type="x-p"/> Pisce Venus latuit, Cyllenius ibidis alis. <div eID="gen2631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2632" type="x-p"/> Metam., l. v., fab. v., 1. 326. <div eID="gen2632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2633" type="x-p"/> How the gods fled to Egypt's slimy soil, <div eID="gen2633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2634" type="x-p"/> And hid their heads beneath the banks of Nile; <div eID="gen2634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2635" type="x-p"/> How Typhon from the conquer'd skies pursued <div eID="gen2635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2636" type="x-p"/> Their routed godheads to the seven-mouth'd flood; <div eID="gen2636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2637" type="x-p"/> Forced every god, his fury to escape, <div eID="gen2637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2638" type="x-p"/> Some beastly form to take, or earthly shape. <div eID="gen2638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2639" type="x-p"/> Jove, so she sung, was changed into a ram, <div eID="gen2639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2640" type="x-p"/> From whence the horns of Libyan Ammon came; <div eID="gen2640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2641" type="x-p"/> Bacchus a goat, Apollo was a crow, <div eID="gen2641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2642" type="x-p"/> Phoebe a cat, the wife of Jove a cow, <div eID="gen2642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2643" type="x-p"/> Whose hue was whiter than the falling snow; <div eID="gen2643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2644" type="x-p"/> Mercury, to a nasty ibis turn'd, <div eID="gen2644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2645" type="x-p"/> The change obscene, afraid of Typhon mourn'd, <div eID="gen2645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2646" type="x-p"/> While Venus from a fish protection craves, <div eID="gen2646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2647" type="x-p"/> And once more plunges in her native waves - Maynwaring. <div eID="gen2647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2648" type="x-p"/> These animals therefore became sacred to them on account of the deities, who, as the fable reports, had taken refuge in them. Others suppose that the reason why the Egyptians would not sacrifice or kill those creatures was their belief in the doctrine of the metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls; for they feared lest in killing an animal they should kill a relative or a friend. This doctrine is still held by the Hindoos.
entries.020360cbc92fffc3cea47d1ed325287246f11ee6: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen2648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2649" type="x-p"/> And sacrifice to the Lord - as he shall command us - It is very likely that neither Moses nor Aaron knew as yet in what manner God would be worshipped; and they expected to receive a direct revelation from him relative to this subject, when they should come into the wilderness.
entries.ed1adee357052f1b6b0a351235941a9087f669d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen2649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2650" type="x-p"/> I will let you go only ye shall not go very far away - Pharaoh relented because the hand of God was heavy upon him; but he was not willing to give up his gain. The Israelites were very profitable to him; they were slaves of the state, and their hard labor was very productive: hence he professed a willingness, first to tolerate their religion in the land, (<reference osisRef="Exo.8.25">Exo 8:25</reference>); or to permit them to go into the wilderness, so that they went not far away, and would soon return. How ready is foolish man, when the hand of God presses him sore, to compound with his Maker! He will consent to give up some sins, provided God will permit him to keep others. <div eID="gen2650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2651" type="x-p"/> Entreat for me - Exactly similar to the case of Simon Magus, who, like Pharaoh, fearing the Divine judgments, begged an interest in the prayers of Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.8.24">Act 8:24</reference>.
entries.566fb465d5d2024d1cfdcab4a146f288e928405e: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen2651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2652" type="x-p"/> The Lord did according to the word of Moses - How powerful is prayer! God permits his servant to prescribe even the manner and time in which he shall work. <div eID="gen2652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2653" type="x-p"/> He removed the swarms - Probably by means of a strong wind, which swept them into the sea.
entries.6daf057ed60cdddef98114ec92c6adb49f3d902d: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen2653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2654" type="x-p"/> Pharaoh hardened his heart at this time also - See <reference osisRef="Exo.8.15">Exo 8:15</reference>. This hardening was the mere effect of his self-determining obstinacy. He preferred his gain to the will and command of Jehovah, and God made his obstinacy the means of showing forth his own power and providence in a supereminent degree. <div eID="gen2654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2655" type="x-p"/> 1. As every false religion proves there is a true one, as a copy, however marred or imperfect, shows there was an original from which it was taken, so false miracles prove that there were genuine miracles, and that God chooses at particular times, for the most important purposes, to invert the established order of nature, and thus prove his omnipotence and universal agency. That the miracles wrought at this time were real we have the fullest proof. The waters, for instance, were not turned into blood in appearance merely, but were really thus changed. Hence the people could not drink of them; and as blood in a very short time, when exposed to the air, becomes putrid, so did the bloody waters; therefore all the fish that were in the river died. <div eID="gen2655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> 2. No human power or ingenuity could produce such frogs as annoyed the land of Egypt. This also was a real, not an imaginary, plague. Innumerable multitudes of these animals were produced for the purpose; and the heaps of their dead carcasses, which putrefied and infected the land, at once demonstrated the reality of the miracle. <div eID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2657" type="x-p"/> 3. The lice both on man and beast through the whole land, and the innumerable swarms of flies, gave such proofs of their reality as to put the truth of these miracles out of question for ever. It was necessary that this point should be fully proved, that both the Egyptians and Israelites might see the finger of God in these awful works. <div eID="gen2657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> 4. To superficial observers only do "Moses and the magicians appear to be nearly matched." The power of God was shown in producing and removing the plagues. In certain cases the magicians imitated the production of a plague, but they had no power to remove any. They could not seem to remove the bloody color, nor the putrescency from the waters through which the fish were destroyed, though they could imitate the color itself; they could not remove the frogs, the lice, or swarms of flies, though they could imitate the former and latter; they could by dexterity of hand or diabolic influence produce serpents, but they could not bring one forward that could swallow up the rod of Aaron. In every respect they fall infinitely short of the power and wonderful energy evidenced in the miracles of Moses and Aaron. The opposition therefore of those men served only as a foil to set off the excellence of that power by which these messengers of God acted. <div eID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> 5. The courage, constancy, and faith of Moses are worthy of the most serious consideration. Had he not been fully satisfied of the truth and certainty of his Divine mission, he could not have encountered such a host of difficulties; had he not been certain of the issue, he could not have preserved amidst so many discouraging circumstances; and had he not had a deep acquaintance with God, his faith in every trial must have necessarily failed. So strong was this grace in him that he could even pledge his Maker to the performance of works concerning which he had not as yet consulted him! He therefore let Pharaoh fix the very time on which he would wish to have the plague removed; and when this was done, he went to God by faith and prayer to obtain this new miracle; and God in the most exact and circumstantial manner fulfilled the word of his servant. <div eID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> 6. From all this let us learn that there is a God who worketh in the earth; that universal nature is under his control; that he can alter, suspend, counteract, or invert its general laws whensoever he pleases; and that he can save or destroy by the most feeble and most contemptible instruments. We should therefore deeply reverence his eternal power and Godhead, and look with respect on every creature he has made, as the meanest of them may in his hand, become the instrument of our salvation or our ruin. <div eID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2661" type="x-p"/> 7. Let us not imagine that God has so bound himself to work by general laws, that those destructions cannot take place which designate a particular providence. Pharaoh and the Egyptians are confounded, afflicted, routed, and ruined, while the land of Goshen and the Israelites are free from every plague! No blood appears in their streams; no frogs, lice, nor flies, in all their borders! They trusted in the true God, and could not be confounded. Reader, how secure mayest thou rest if thou hast this God for thy friend! He was the Protector and Friend of the Israelites through the blood of that covenant which is the very charter of thy salvation: trust in and pray to him as Moses did, and then Satan and his angels shall be bruised under thy feet, and thou shalt not only be preserved from every plague, but be crowned with his loving kindness and tender mercy. He is the same to-day that he was yesterday, and shall continue the same for ever. Hallelujah, the Lord God omnipotent reigneth!  <chapter eID="Exod.8"/> <div eID="gen2661" type="x-p"/>

entries.3bbeb1b9d34c9fc7a8a14be4c9e8f54f528af080: <reference osisRef="Exod.8.1-Exod.8.6">Exo 8:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen705" type="x-p"/> The plague of Frogs, or the <hi type="italic">second</hi> plague, also proceeded from the Nile, and had its natural origin in the putridity of the slimy Nile water, whereby the marsh waters especially became filled with thousands of frogs. צפרדּע is the small Nile frog, the <hi type="italic">Dofda</hi> of the Egyptians, called <hi type="italic">rana Mosaica</hi> or <hi type="italic">Nilotica</hi> by <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, which appears in large numbers as soon as the waters recede. These frogs (הצּפרדּע in <reference osisRef="Exod.8.6">Exo 8:6</reference>, used collectively) became a penal miracle from the fact that they came out of the water in unparalleled numbers, in consequence of the stretching out of Aaron’s staff over the waters of the Nile, as had been foretold to the king, and that they not only penetrated into the houses and inner rooms (“bed-chamber”), and crept into the domestic utensils, the beds (מטּה), the ovens, and the kneading-troughs (not the “dough” as <hi type="italic">Luther</hi> renders it), but even got upon the men themselves.
entries.2beaeed338d3e2adf6429680acdc38f085f069fe: <reference osisRef="Exod.8.7-Exod.8.9">Exo 8:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen706" type="x-p"/> This miracle was also imitated by the Egyptian augurs with their secret arts, and frogs were brought upon the land by them. But if they were able to bring the plague, they could not take it away. The latter is not expressly stated, it is true; but it is evident from the fact that Pharaoh was obliged to send for Moses and Aaron to intercede with Jehovah to take them away. The king would never have applied to Moses and Aaron for help if his charmers could have charmed the plague away. Moreover the fact that Pharaoh entreated them to intercede with Jehovah to take away the frogs, and promised to let the people go, that they might sacrifice to Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.8">Exo 8:8</reference>), was a sign that he regarded the God of Israel as the author of the plague. To strengthen the impression made upon the king by this plague with reference to the might of Jehovah, Moses said to him (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.9">Exo 8:9</reference>), “<hi type="italic">Glorify thyself over me, when I shall entreat for thee,</hi>” i.e., take the glory upon thyself of determining the time when I shall remove the plague through my intercession. The expression is elliptical, and לעמר (saying) is to be supplied, as in Jdg 7:2. To give Jehovah the glory, Moses placed himself below Pharaoh, and left him to fix the time for the frogs to be removed through his intercession.
entries.c544d38c779c7cde699adaf94836067f5c4bb0cc: <reference osisRef="Exod.8.10-Exod.8.15">Exo 8:10-15</reference> <div eID="gen706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen707" type="x-p"/> The king appointed the following day, probably because he hardly thought it possible for so great a work to be performed at once. Moses promised that it should be so: “<hi type="italic">According to thy word</hi> (sc., let it be), <hi type="italic">that thou mayest know that there is not</hi> (a God) <hi type="italic">like Jehovah our God</hi>.” He then went out and cried, i.e., called aloud and earnestly, to Jehovah concerning the matter (דּבר על) of the frogs, which he had set, i.e., prepared, for Pharaoh (שׂוּם as in <reference osisRef="Gen.45.7">Gen 45:7</reference>). In consequence of his intercession God took the plague away. The frogs died off (מן מוּת, to die away out of, from), out of the houses, and palaces, and fields, and were gathered together by bushels (חמרים from חמר, the <hi type="italic">omer</hi>, the largest measure used by the Hebrews), so that the land stank with the odour of their putrefaction. Though Jehovah had thus manifested Himself as the Almighty God and Lord of the creation, Pharaoh did not keep his promise; but when he saw that there was breathing-time (רוחה, ἀνάψυξις, relief from an overpowering pressure), literally, as soon as he “<hi type="italic">got air,</hi>” he hardened his heart, so that he did not hearken to Moses and Aaron (והכבּד <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>).
entries.90a0b896ce5ba21e0a944b89198ff19aa5e1da2b: <reference osisRef="Exod.8.16-Exod.8.17">Exo 8:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen708" type="x-p"/> The Gnats, or the third plague. - The כּנּם, or כּנּים (also כּנּם, probably an old singular form, <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §163 <hi type="italic">f</hi>), were not “<hi type="italic">lice,</hi>” but σκνῖφες, <hi type="italic">sciniphes</hi>, a species of gnats, so small as to be hardly visible to the eye, but with a sting which, according to <hi type="italic">Philo</hi> and <hi type="italic">Origen</hi>, causes a most painful irritation of the skin.
